characters.hamo: Hamo is the warm uncle of Sêvan, a village of apple orchards below the mountains, and the main voice of the road. Steady, patient and easily pleased, he laughs at his own stories (often before the end of them), lifts the near end of his full black moustache when he is pleased with you, and is proudest of that moustache above everything he owns. A miss gets one raised brow and a thoughtful look, never a cross word. He wears the traditional suit with a green pştên, keeps the orchard, drinks tea from dawn to dusk, is never quite on time, and knows a proverb or a tale for every moment. He is Xezal’s maternal uncle (her xal), husband of Nazê, father of Baran and Hêvî, and son of Dapîr Şemsê.
characters.xezo: Xezal is Hamo’s niece, the daughter of his sister Gulîstan. She lives in Amed, studies at the university there and comes to the village to visit; Hamo calls her Xezo, which she pretends to hate. Bright, quick and a little cheeky, she teases her uncle about his moustache and his timekeeping, giggles with her shoulders, tilts her head to listen and winks when you get something right; a miss gets a short pout that is gone in a moment, because she is on your side. She knows the city and the village alike, bargains better than anyone at the market, and in the last units has to decide whether to take a teaching post far away in Hewlêr.
characters.hevalo: Hevalo is the young deer who is the learner’s guide: he brings you to Hamo’s gate in the first lesson and walks the whole road beside you. His name means “O friend!”, which Xezal finds very funny. Curious about everything and quick on his feet, he hops when he is pleased, tilts his head when something puzzles him and pricks up both ears at anything new. He is always hungry for apples and always the first suspect when apples go missing, cheeky in a sweet way and kind when you get something wrong. He speaks little — a guide’s word here and there — and on the summer pastures he meets Zerê, a shy wild doe, and gives her his last apple.

units.story: You step off the bus at the edge of Sêvan, a village of apple orchards under the mountains, with Hevalo the young deer as your guide. At a blue gate Hamo welcomes you — the warm uncle with the proudest moustache in the valley. Before the tea is even poured, his niece Xezal runs up the lane from the Amed bus, and Hamo calls her Xezo, which she pretends to hate. Over four small scenes you learn to say hello, to say who you are and where you are from, and to ask how everyone is — while Hevalo keeps disappearing towards the apple trees.

skills.grammar: the personal pronouns ez and tu, and the present copula: ez … im / me, tu … î / yî, ew … e / ye
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez baş im** — I am well. In Kurmancî “to be” is not a word of its own: it is a small ending put after the word it describes.

- **ez … im** (after a consonant) / **ez … me** (after a vowel): *Ez baş im.* I am well. · *Ez Hamo me.* I am Hamo.
- **tu … î / yî**: *Tu mêvan î.* You are a guest. · *Tu Hevalo yî?* Are you Hevalo?
- **ew … e / ye**: *Ew birçî ye.* He is hungry. · *Çay germ e.* The tea is hot.

The verb always comes last, so a sentence ends with its little “am / are / is”. A question sounds like a statement with your voice going up: *Tu baş î?* — Are you well?

lessons.beat: Hevalo leads you up a lane of apple trees to a blue gate. It swings open and a man with a magnificent black moustache beams at you: “Silav!”

new.en: am (im after a consonant, me after a vowel)

lessons.beat: “Ez Hamo me,” he says, and gives the end of his moustache a proud little lift. Hevalo introduces you as a guest and a friend — and Hamo laughs: the deer’s own name means “friend!”

new.en: are (with tu: î after a consonant, yî after a vowel)

lessons.beat: Hamo welcomes you properly at the gate, and you learn the answer that every guest gives. Hevalo is not listening: he has seen the apple tree.

new.en: Thank you! (the answer to a welcome: may you stay well)
is (e after a consonant, ye after a vowel)
here you are; please, go ahead

lessons.beat: Hamo pours the first glass of tea of your stay and blows on his own. Then a voice shouts “Xalo! Xalo!” from the bottom of the lane — someone is running up the hill.

skills.grammar: giving and asking names: navê min … e, navê te çi ye?, and who someone is with kî
skills.grammarMd:
To give your name, say **Navê min … e** — literally “the name of me is …”.

- *Navê min Xezal e.* My name is Xezal.
- *Navê min Hamo ye.* My name is Hamo. (**ye** after a vowel)
- *Navê te çi ye?* What is your name?

**navê** is *nav* (name) with the ending **-ê** that links it to *min* (me) or *te* (you) — you will meet that link properly in the next unit.

To say what someone is **not**, put **ne** before the word: *Ez ne Xezo me!* I am not Xezo! · *Ew ne mêvan e.* She is not a guest.
To ask who: *Ew kî ye?* Who is that?

lessons.beat: A young woman with a huge bag runs up the lane: Hamo’s niece from Amed. “Silav! Navê min Xezal e!” Hamo hugs her: “Ew Xezo ye!” — “Xezal, Xalo!”
Xezal asks your name and the deer’s. When she hears “Hevalo” she laughs so hard she has to sit down on her bag: a deer called “Friend!”

new.en: not (with the copula: ez ne … im)

lessons.beat: Introductions round the tea tray. Hamo keeps calling his niece Xezo; she keeps correcting him; he laughs at his own joke for the third time — and so, in the end, does she.
Hamo names everyone in the yard — the dog, the donkey, even the hens. Then he looks round: “Hevalo li ku ye?” The deer has vanished.

skills.grammar: ji ku derê?: where someone is from; a place after ji takes -ê (ji Amedê, ji Sêvanê)
skills.grammarMd:
**Tu ji ku derê yî?** — Where are you from? (literally “you from which place are?”)

The answer uses **ji** (from) and the place, which takes **-ê**:

- *Ez ji Amedê me.* I am from Amed.
- *Ez ji Sêvanê me.* I am from Sêvan.
- *Ew ji Almanyayê ye.* She is from Germany.

A place that ends in a vowel adds **-yê**: *ji Almanyayê*, *ji Sineyê*. The copula after it is **me / yî / ye** because the word before it now ends in a vowel.

**li** means *in, at*: *Ez li gund im.* I am in the village. · *Hevalo li baxçe ye.* Hevalo is in the orchard.

lessons.beat: Everyone hunts for the deer. You find Hevalo in the orchard under the oldest apple tree, his cheeks suspiciously round.
Back at the tea, Hamo says he has been from Sêvan all his life; Xezal is from the city; and you — you have come from far away to learn Kurdish.
Xezal says Amed is the most beautiful place in the world; Hamo says Sêvan is; Hevalo, with his mouth full, says the apples are.
Everyone says where they are from, and you say it best of all. Then a neighbour appears at the gate with a covered basket and a mysterious smile: “Ew mêvan kî ye?”

skills.grammar: the plural pronouns em, hûn, ew and the copula in / ne; asking how someone is with çawa
skills.grammarMd:
**Tu çawa yî?** — How are you? **Ez baş im, spas.** — I am well, thanks.

For more than one person the copula is **in** (after a consonant) or **ne** (after a vowel):

- *Em baş in.* We are well.
- *Hûn çawa ne?* How are you (all)? — **hûn** is also the polite “you” to one older person.
- *Ew birçî ne.* They are hungry.

So the whole set is: ez … im/me · tu … î/yî · ew … e/ye · em, hûn, ew … in/ne.

Kurdish greets by the time of day: *Roj baş!* Good day! · *Êvar baş!* Good evening! · *Şev baş!* Good night!

lessons.beat: Morning in Sêvan. Hamo asks everyone how they are — you, Xezal, the hens. Hevalo’s answer is always the same: “Ez birçî me.”

new.en: are (with em, hûn, ew: in after a consonant, ne after a vowel)

lessons.beat: Xezal answers for the whole house — “Em hemû baş in!” — and Hevalo protests that he is not well at all: he is hungry. Hamo asks how you really are.

new.en: state, how things are (halê te: how you are)

lessons.beat: Tea under the apple tree as the sun goes down. Hamo tells the story of how his moustache froze one winter, and laughs at it long before the end.
The neighbours say goodbye one by one. At the gate Hamo winks: tomorrow the whole family is coming — and someone Xezal has not seen for years.

new.en: Goodbye! (said by the one who leaves, to one person)
Safe journey! (the answer to “Bi xatirê te!”)

units.story: The whole family gathers at Hamo’s house: his wife Nazê, their son Baran (nine, full of questions), their daughter Hêvî (six, shy until she is not) and Hamo’s mother, Dapîr Şemsê, who knows everybody’s business. The photos come out, the hens are counted, ages are guessed — Dapîr will not tell hers — and Xezal finds the family’s greatest secret: a photo of young Hamo without his moustache. Everyone has something to show: a brother, a sister, a donkey called Bozo. Hevalo has no apples, and says so.

skills.grammar: the ezafe: a noun joined to the word after it with -ê (masculine) or -a (feminine): bavê min, diya min
skills.grammarMd:
In Kurmancî the owner comes **after** the thing, joined by a small ending, the **ezafe**:

- masculine words take **-ê**: *bavê min* my father · *birayê te* your brother · *simbêlê Hamo* Hamo’s moustache
- feminine words take **-a**: *xwişka min* my sister · *malbata me* our family · *jina wî* his wife

**dê** (mother) is irregular: *diya min* my mother, and you call her *Dayê!*

The pronouns after the ezafe are the “object” ones: **min, te, wî** (his), **wê** (her), **me, we, wan**.

Every noun is masculine or feminine, and the ending tells you which: learn *sêva min* and *nanê min* together with the words.

lessons.beat: Hamo shows you the photo wall in the guest room: “Ev bavê min e. Ev diya min e.” His father wears the same moustache, only grander.
Nazê comes out with warm bread. “Ev jina min e,” says Hamo. “Û ev mêrê min e,” says Nazê, “û simbêlê wî.” Dapîr Şemsê follows, leaning on her stick and on everyone.
Xezal finds an old photo behind the others: a young man with no moustache at all. “Ev kî ye?” Hamo goes red. Dapîr laughs until she cries: it is Hamo.
Hamo makes everyone promise to keep the photo a secret — but Hevalo has already chewed a corner of it. Then Baran bursts in: Bozo the donkey is gone from the stable!

skills.grammar: the plural ezafe -ên, the ezafe after a vowel (-yê, -ya, -yên), and yê / ya / yên on their own: ya min, mine
skills.grammarMd:
For **plural** owners and things the ezafe is **-ên**: *birayên min* my brothers · *zarokên me* our children.

After a **vowel**, a **y** slips in: *birayê min* my brother · *xwarziya min* my niece · *wêneyên me* our photos.

The ezafe can also stand alone, meaning “the one of”:

- *Ev pêlav ya min e.* This shoe is mine. (**ya** for a feminine thing)
- *Ev kum yê te ye.* This cap is yours. (**yê** for a masculine thing)
- *Ev pirtûk yên wan in.* These books are theirs. (**yên** for plural)

To ask whose: *Ev ya kê ye?* Whose is this?

lessons.beat: Hevalo follows his nose and finds Bozo in Dapîr’s flower bed, eating her roses one by one. Dapîr is not amused; Bozo is delighted.
Hamo introduces his children properly. Baran: “Ez kurê mezin im!” Hêvî hides behind Dapîr. And Xezal explains who is whose cousin, which takes a while.

new.en: cousin (the son of your father’s brother)
cousin (the daughter of your father’s sister)
cousin (the son of your mother’s brother)

lessons.beat: A mountain of shoes at the door. Xezal sorts them out: the biggest pair is Hamo’s, the tiniest Hêvî’s, and nothing at all is Hevalo’s.

new.en: whose; whom (kî after a preposition or the ezafe)

lessons.beat: Dapîr Şemsê holds court in the best cushion. She asks about your family, and says she has a present for the guest — but only after she has counted to twenty.

skills.grammar: the numbers from one to twenty before the noun (sê sêv), çend? (how many?) and age with salî
skills.grammarMd:
The number comes **before** the noun, and the noun stays as it is: *sê sêv* three apples · *du bira* two brothers.

1 yek · 2 du · 3 sê · 4 çar · 5 pênc · 6 şeş · 7 heft · 8 heşt · 9 neh · 10 deh

The teens build on deh: *yazdeh, diwanzdeh, sêzdeh … nozdeh*, and 20 is *bîst*.

Ask **çend?** for how many: *Çend sêv hene?* How many apples are there?

Age uses **salî** (years old): *Tu çend salî yî?* How old are you? · *Ez neh salî me.* I am nine. · *Hêvî şeş salî ye.* Hêvî is six.

lessons.beat: Dapîr counts the hens with Hêvî. They get a different number every time, because the hens will not stand still.
Hamo counts apples into a basket for Dapîr’s present. Seven, eight, nine… and somehow it is always one fewer. Hevalo looks at the sky.
Ages round the table: Baran is nine, Hêvî six, Xezal nineteen. Dapîr says firmly that she is twenty, and nobody dares to argue.
Dapîr counts slowly to twenty and opens her old chest: inside is a pair of knitted socks — no, four, in Hevalo’s size — and an old key nobody recognises.

skills.grammar: having with heye / hene / tune (Birayekî min heye), and the indefinite -ek with the ezafe: -ekî (masculine), -eke (feminine)
skills.grammarMd:
Kurmancî says “I have” as “of me there is”: **… min heye**.

- *Birayekî min heye.* I have a brother.
- *Du xwişkên min hene.* I have two sisters. (**hene** for more than one)
- *Pisîka min tune.* I don’t have a cat.

**-ek** means *a, one*: *sêvek* an apple. Joined to the owner it becomes **-ekî** for a masculine word and **-eke** for a feminine one: *kurekî min* a son of mine · *xwişkeke te* a sister of yours.

**heye** also means *there is*: *Li baxçe sêv hene.* There are apples in the orchard.

lessons.beat: Hamo tells you about his family: “Xwişkeke min heye — diya Xezalê.” He has no brother, but he has a horse, a cow and a whole flock of sheep.
Xezal shows a photo of her cat Gewrê, at home in Amed. Baran tops it at once: “Kerekî me heye: Bozo!”
A game at dinner: everyone says one thing they have and one they don’t. Hevalo: “Sêveke min tune!” So everyone gives him one — and now he has six.
Dapîr’s key opens a dusty box under the stairs. Inside: Hamo’s first moustache comb — and a folded map of the village with an X drawn on it in a child’s hand.

units.story: With the child’s map from the old box, Xezal, Hevalo and you search for the spot marked X: through every room of the house, past the blue doors and white walls of the village, up on the roof and down by the spring — while Hamo swears he knows nothing and grins under his moustache. Someone else is searching too: a fresh X appears on a windowsill. Under the walnut tree by the spring the treasure is found at last — marbles, and half of an old photo of young Hamo and his sister Gulîstan. Where is the other half? In Amed. And tomorrow is market day.

skills.grammar: this and that: ev / ew, and after a preposition vî / vê / van, wî / wê / wan (li vê odeyê, di wî xanî de)
skills.grammarMd:
**ev** means *this, these* and **ew** *that, those* — when they are the subject:

- *Ev ode ye.* This is a room. · *Ew derî şîn e.* That door is blue.

After a preposition (li, ji, di … de, bi) they change, and so does the noun:

- masculine: **vî / wî** + **-î**: *di vî xanî de* in this house · *li wî gundî* in that village
- feminine: **vê / wê** + **-ê**: *li vê odeyê* in this room · *ji wê malê* from that house
- plural: **van / wan** + **-an**: *li van gundan* in these villages

This changed form is the **oblique**. You already know it from *ji Amedê* and *li malê*.

lessons.beat: Hamo gives you the house tour with great ceremony, as if you were a visiting governor: “Ev ode ye. Ew jî derî ye.”
In every room something is out of place — a hen in the kitchen, a shoe on the table — and the map, it turns out, has been upside down all morning.

new.en: this, these (after a preposition: li vê malê)
that, those (after a preposition: li wê malê)

lessons.beat: Xezal and you read the map together: the house is there, the spring is there, and the X is outside. Hamo “innocently” offers to help — and points the wrong way.
The whole house is mapped and named. Then Hevalo sniffs at the window: on the sill someone has scratched a second X — and it is fresh. Someone else is looking too.

skills.grammar: adjectives after the noun, joined with the ezafe: deriyê şîn, mala spî, sêvên sor
skills.grammarMd:
An adjective comes **after** its noun, joined by the same ezafe you know from *navê min*:

- *derî* + *şîn* → **deriyê şîn** the blue door
- *mal* + *spî* → **mala spî** the white house
- *sêv* + *sor* → **sêvên sor** (the) red apples

With **a**: *deriyekî şîn* a blue door · *maleke spî* a white house.

As a description after the copula there is no ezafe: *Derî şîn e.* The door is blue. · *Sêv sor in.* The apples are red.

The colours: *sor* red · *şîn* blue · *kesk* green · *zer* yellow · *reş* black · *spî* white · *qehweyî* brown · *gewr* grey.

lessons.beat: Hamo teaches you the colours from his own garden: red apples, blue gate, green leaves, yellow sun, black moustache, white beard (Dapîr’s goat’s).
The map’s next clue is “a blue door by a white wall”. Xezal is triumphant — until she counts three blue doors in the village.
Hamo and Xezal argue: red apples or green ones? Hevalo settles it the only way a deer can — he eats one of each. Then he spots the next clue on a tree.
The colours lead to the old walnut tree by the spring — but whose fresh X was on the window? Hêvî giggles behind her hands. She knows something.

skills.grammar: where things are: li ser, li bin, li ber, li pişt, li kêleka, li cem, di … de, di nav … de
skills.grammarMd:
**li** (at, in) combines with a word for the place:

- **li ser** on · **li bin** under · **li ber** in front of · **li pişt** behind · **li kêleka** next to · **li cem** at someone’s place

*Berçavk li ser serê te ye!* The glasses are on your head!

**di … de** wraps around the noun for *inside*: *di sindoqê de* in the box · *di metbexê de* in the kitchen. **di nav … de** is *among, in the middle of*: *di nav daran de* among the trees.

The noun after them takes the oblique: feminine **-ê** (*li bin darê* under the tree), plural **-an** (*li ser keviran*); a masculine noun usually stays as it is (*li ser kevir*, *li ber derî*).

lessons.beat: Hamo cannot find his glasses anywhere: not on the table, not under the bed, not behind the door. They are on his head.
Hamo reads out the map’s last clue, in the corner in his own childhood hand (he still claims he has never seen it): “di nav keviran de, li kêleka kaniyê” — among the stones, next to the spring.
At the walnut tree by the spring Hamo “remembers” nothing. Xezal searches under stones and behind the trunk; Hevalo digs eagerly — and finds an apple core. His own, from yesterday.
Under the flat stone: a tin with marbles and half of an old photo — little Hamo and his sister. Hamo confesses he hid it with Gulîstan thirty years ago. The other half? “Li cem wê ye. Li Amedê.”

skills.grammar: plurals: a plural noun alone has no ending (du mal), -ên with the ezafe (malên spî), -an after a preposition (li gundan); gelek, çend, hemû, her
skills.grammarMd:
A Kurdish plural often looks like the singular: *Du mal hene.* There are two houses. · *Sêv sor in.* The apples are red.

You see the plural in the endings:

- with the ezafe: **-ên**: *malên spî* the white houses · *zarokên gund* the village children
- after a preposition: **-an**: *li gundan* in the villages · *ji zarokan re* for the children

Counting words: *gelek mal* many houses · *çend dar* a few trees · *hemû zarok* all the children · *her roj* every day (her takes the singular).

**kes** is a person; with a negative it means nobody: *Kes li malê tune.* There is nobody at home.

lessons.beat: Hamo walks you through the village: the school, Ferhad’s little shop, the square, the old mill and the vineyards that climb the hill.
From the roof Hamo counts the village: forty houses, two hundred trees (he says), one school, one shepherd and far too many hens.
Xezal and you in the square: the neighbours want to know who you are. Ferhad has news — tomorrow is market day in the town, and everyone is going.
Hamo writes a shopping list in enormous letters; Hevalo adds “sêv” ten times. And Bozo the donkey refuses to go anywhere without his hat.

units.story: Market day in the town below the village. Hamo, Xezal, Hevalo and you ride down with Bozo, who is wearing his hat. The present tense comes alive as everyone goes, comes, looks, wants, buys and eats. Mîrza the fruit seller and Hamo haggle like the old friends they are — though Mîrza swears Hamo still owes him for a melon from twenty years ago — and Xezal bargains better than both of them. Then Mîrza’s apple crate is found empty, every witness says “Ez nizanim”, and a certain deer has a very round belly. On the way home Xezal gets a phone call: she must go back to Amed on Saturday, and her mother wants everyone to come.

skills.titleEn: I am going to the market
skills.grammar: the present tense: di- + present stem + -im, -î, -e, -in, with the irregular stems diç- (çûn), tê- (hatin), dik- (kirin), dibîn- (dîtin), dibêj- (gotin), dizan- (zanîn), did- (dan)
skills.grammarMd:
The present tense is **di-** + the verb’s present stem + a personal ending:

| | çûn (go) | kirin (do) |
|---|---|---|
| ez | diçim | dikim |
| tu | diçî | dikî |
| ew | diçe | dike |
| em, hûn, ew | diçin | dikin |

The stem is often not what the dictionary form suggests, so learn the **ez** form with each verb: *dîtin → dibînim* (see), *gotin → dibêjim* (say), *dan → didim* (give), *zanîn → dizanim* (know).

**hatin** (come) has no di-: *ez têm, tu têyî, ew tê, em tên*.

A place you go to takes -ê and needs no preposition: *Ez diçim bazarê.* I am going to the market.

lessons.beat: Bozo, in his hat, carries the empty baskets down the hill. Hamo walks in front, Xezal behind, Hevalo everywhere: “Em diçin bazarê!”
On the way Hamo points out everything he sees and says something about all of it. Bozo stops at every flower and says nothing.

new.en: to look (li … nêrîn: to look at)

lessons.beat: The market roars with voices. Hamo knows every seller and tells you who sells what, then hugs Mîrza like a long-lost brother; Hevalo says he is “only looking” at the apples.

new.en: to walk around; li … gerîn: to look for

lessons.beat: Over tea Hamo and Mîrza tell old stories. Then Mîrza remembers: Hamo still owes him for a watermelon — from twenty years ago.

new.en: to like, to love (ji … hez kirin)

skills.grammar: more irregular presents: dixwazim (xwestin), dixwim (xwarin), vedixwim (vexwarin), dikarim (karîn)
skills.grammarMd:
Four verbs you will use every day:

- **xwestin** want: *ez dixwazim, tu dixwazî, ew dixwaze, em dixwazin*
- **xwarin** eat: *ez dixwim, tu dixwî, ew dixwe, em dixwin*
- **vexwarin** drink: *ez vedixwim, tu vedixwî, ew vedixwe* — the **ve-** stays in front of di-
- **karîn** can: *ez dikarim, tu dikarî, ew dikare*

The object comes before the verb: *Ez nan dixwim.* I am eating bread. · *Tu çay vedixwî?* Are you drinking tea? · *Hevalo sêv dixwaze.* Hevalo wants an apple.

**ji … hez dikim** is “I like”: *Ez ji penîr hez dikim.* I like cheese.

lessons.beat: Hamo reads the list aloud at the vegetable stall: tomatoes, potatoes, onions — and whatever else he sees on the way.
Xezal says she can carry everything; she can bargain; she can find the best honey in the market. Hamo strokes his moustache: “Tu dikarî? Baş e!”
Hamo orders cheese, honey and olives; Mîrza pours tea; Xezal wants pomegranates; and Hevalo wants — you can guess.
Lunch on a bench: bread, cheese and tea. Everyone is eating — except Hevalo, which is suspicious. Then Mîrza shouts from his stall: “Sêvên min li ku ne?!”

skills.grammar: the numbers to a thousand (bîst û yek, sed, du sed û pêncî, hezar) and prices with bi: bi çend e?, bi sed e
skills.grammarMd:
The tens: *bîst* 20 · *sî* 30 · *çil* 40 · *pêncî* 50 · *şêst* 60 · *heftê* 70 · *heştê* 80 · *not* 90 · *sed* 100 · *hezar* 1000.

Join the parts with **û**, biggest first: *bîst û yek* 21 · *sed û pêncî* 150 · *du sed û heştê û pênc* 285 · *hezar û du sed* 1200.

For prices use **bi** (for): *Ev bi çend e?* How much is this? · *Kîloyek bi pêncî ye.* It is fifty a kilo. · *Ez vê bi sî dikirim.* I’ll buy it for thirty.

*biha* expensive · *erzan* cheap · *Pir biha ye!* It is too expensive!

lessons.beat: Hamo reads the prices on the stalls aloud, and is shocked by every one of them. “Pêncî?! Na, na, na!”
Xezal does the sums for the whole list on her phone and announces the total: Hamo pretends to faint into Bozo’s baskets.
Hamo and Mîrza haggle over a copper teapot: “Bi sed û pêncî!” — “Na, bi sed!” Xezal steps in, smiles sweetly, and gets it for eighty. Mîrza laughs and gives in.
Hamo pays for everything and counts his change three times. Then Mîrza looks at his apple crate and goes pale: it is empty.

skills.grammar: negation in the present: na- replaces di- (naçim, nakim, nayêm), ni- for zanîn and karîn (nizanim, nikarim), ne before the copula
skills.grammarMd:
To say *not*, put **na-** where **di-** was:

- *Ez diçim → Ez naçim.* I am not going.
- *Ew dixwe → Ew naxwe.* He isn’t eating.
- *Tu têyî → Tu nayî.* You aren’t coming. (hatin: *nayêm, nayî, nayê, nayên*)
- *vedixwim → venaxwim* — ve- stays in front.

Two verbs take **ni-**: *nizanim* I don’t know · *nikarim* I can’t.

With the copula use **ne**: *Ez ne birçî me.* I am not hungry.

**qet** is *(not) at all, never*: *Ez qet nizanim!* I have no idea!

lessons.beat: The great apple mystery. Mîrza asks everyone. Bozo looks away. Hevalo, very quickly: “Ez nizanim! Ez qet nizanim!”

new.en: not (with zanîn and karîn: nizanim, nikarim)

lessons.beat: Xezal questions Hevalo like a detective. Is he hungry? “Na, ez ne birçî me.” Then why is his belly so round? “Ez nizanim.” Then why…? “Hê na!”
The apple trial in the middle of the market: Mîrza is the judge, Xezal the lawyer, the witnesses know nothing — and the accused has apple on his nose. Hamo pays for the apples, laughing.
Home at sunset, Bozo groaning under the bags. Xezal’s phone rings: she must go back to Amed on Saturday — and her mother wants the whole family to come too.

units.story: Xezal has to be back in Amed on Saturday, so the whole family plans the week around her: the days on Dapîr’s wall calendar fill up, the months and birthdays are argued over (Hamo does not know his own — “the year of the big snow”), and the clock becomes the week’s great enemy. Hamo’s day runs on tea: up with the rooster, tea, the orchard, tea, a nap, tea. He promises to be on time for the Saturday bus. On Saturday morning his alarm rings at eight — in the evening — and the family arrives in the square just in time to see the bus disappear round the bend.

skills.grammar: the days of the week, counted from Saturday (Şemî, Yekşem … În); roja Duşemê, îro, sibe, duh, dusibe
skills.grammarMd:
The Kurdish week starts on **Şemî** (Saturday), and the next five days count from it:

*Şemî* Saturday · *Yekşem* Sunday (“one after”) · *Duşem* Monday · *Sêşem* Tuesday · *Çarşem* Wednesday · *Pêncşem* Thursday · *În* Friday

Days are written with a capital. “On Monday” is **roja Duşemê** or just **Duşemê**: *Ez roja Înê têm.* I am coming on Friday.

- *Îro Sêşem e.* Today is Tuesday.
- *Sibe Çarşem e.* Tomorrow is Wednesday.
- *Duh* yesterday · *dusibe* the day after tomorrow

To ask when: **kengî?** — *Tu kengî diçî?* When are you leaving?

lessons.beat: Dapîr’s calendar hangs by the stove. Hamo explains the week to you, starting — as every Kurdish week does — on Saturday, which happens to be the day Xezal leaves.
Hamo goes through the rest of the week: Wednesday is bread day, Thursday is Dapîr’s visit to the neighbours, and Friday — Friday is for rest, he says, and for tea.
Xezal tells Baran she leaves on Saturday. Baran protests loudly; Hêvî hides Xezal’s shoes. Hamo settles it: “Şemiyê? Em hemû bi te re tên!”
Everyone writes their plans on the calendar; Hamo writes “çay” on every day. Then Dapîr circles 21 March in red: “Newroz — û tiştekî nû jî.” Newroz, and something new as well.

skills.grammar: the months as the words pages give them (Kanûna Paşîn … Kanûna Pêşîn), the ordinals yekem, duyem, sêyem, and dates (21ê Adarê)
skills.grammarMd:
The months on the wall calendar:

*Kanûna Paşîn* January · *Sibat* February · *Adar* March · *Nîsan* April · *Gulan* May · *Hezîran* June · *Tîrmeh* July · *Tebax* August · *Îlon* September · *Cotmeh* October · *Mijdar* November · *Kanûna Pêşîn* December

“In March” is **di Adarê de** or **meha Adarê**. A date puts the number first with **-ê**: *21ê Adarê* the 21st of March.

Ordinals add **-em** (after a vowel **-yem**): *yekem* first · *duyem* second · *sêyem* third · *dehem* tenth. They go before the noun: *cara yekem* the first time · *roja duyem* the second day.

lessons.beat: Hamo names the spring months as if they were old friends: Adar brings Newroz, Nîsan the blossom, Gulan the roses — and Hezîran the first cherries.
The summer and autumn months: Tîrmeh is too hot for work, Tebax is for the summer pastures, Îlon for the grapes. Baran asks why there is no month for apples. Hevalo agrees.
Baran asks everyone’s birthday. Xezal’s is in Gulan; Nazê’s in Îlon; Hamo does not know his own. Dapîr: “Sala berfa mezin!” — the year of the big snow.
Hamo and Xezal count the days to Saturday on the calendar. She admits she is nervous: her exam results come out that day too. Hamo tells her not to worry — and promises, once again, to be on time.

skills.grammar: telling the time: saet çend e?, saet sê û nîv e, çar kêm çaryek; di saet heftan de (at seven); sibeh, nîvro, êvar, şev
skills.grammarMd:
**Saet çend e?** What time is it?

- *Saet heft e.* It is seven.
- *Saet heft û nîv e.* It is half past seven.
- *Saet heft û çaryek e.* It is a quarter past seven.
- *Saet heşt kêm çaryek e.* It is a quarter to eight (eight minus a quarter).
- *Saet heft û deh deqîqe ye.* It is ten past seven.

“At seven” is **di saet heftan de** — the number takes the plural oblique -an: *di saet çaran de* at four · *di saet yekê de* at one.

Parts of the day: *sibeh* morning · *nîvro* noon · *piştî nîvro* afternoon · *êvar* evening · *şev* night.

lessons.beat: Hamo owns three clocks, and each of them says a different time. He trusts the one that says it is time for tea.
Hamo describes his day with pride: he wakes with the rooster, gets up when the tea is ready, washes his face at the spring, and — after lunch — sleeps “just five minutes”.

new.en: to sleep, to go to bed

lessons.beat: Xezal times Hamo’s morning with her phone. “Five minutes” is an hour; “I’m coming” is two. Nazê confirms it with a laugh: it has been like this for twenty years.

new.en: waiting (li benda … bûn: to wait for)

lessons.beat: Hamo’s whole day, hour by hour, from tea at seven to tea at nine at night. Then he sets his alarm for the Saturday bus — and, though nobody notices, sets it for the wrong eight o’clock.

skills.grammar: how often: her roj, her gav, gelek caran, carinan, kêm caran, qet; ji … heta …
skills.grammarMd:
How often you do something goes before the verb:

- *Ez her roj çay vedixwim.* I drink tea every day.
- *Hamo her gav dereng e.* Hamo is always late.
- *Em gelek caran diçin bazarê.* We often go to the market.
- *Carinan baran tê.* Sometimes it rains (rain comes).
- *Ez kêm caran zû radizim.* I rarely go to bed early.
- *Ew qet naxwe.* He never eats (it).

**ji … heta …** is *from … until …*: *ji sibehê heta êvarê* from morning till evening · *ji Duşemê heta Înê* from Monday to Friday.

lessons.beat: Hamo admits that he is sometimes late. Nazê coughs. Hamo admits that he is often late. Dapîr coughs. Hamo admits nothing more.

new.en: time, occasion (cara yekem: the first time)

lessons.beat: Xezal describes her week in Amed: the bus at seven, the university, football with her friends on Thursdays, music on Fridays. Baran decides he will live in Amed too.
The family plans the trip to Amed: the bus leaves the square at eight sharp on Saturday. Hamo gives his solemn promise. Everybody looks at Nazê; Nazê looks at the ceiling.

new.en: to take, to hold; to close

lessons.beat: Saturday. The alarm rings — at eight in the evening, set the night before. Everyone runs to the square; Hevalo races after the bus, but it is gone round the bend. How will they get to Amed now?

new.en: now, from now on; (with a negative) no longer

units.story: With the bus gone, Ferhad drives everyone to the main road on his tractor, and a minibus takes them the rest of the way to Amed. The city is Xezal’s world: crowded avenues, the ancient black walls, tall buildings, a bookshop, a bakery and a fourth-floor flat with no lift. Hamo is amazed by everything and gets lost twice. Xezal’s mother Gulîstan, Hamo’s sister, opens her door — and her own tin: the other half of the old photo, and a note in their father’s hand that says something is waiting for them on the hill at Newroz. The imperative is everywhere (were, rûne, bixwe, meke!), and so are divê and dikarim.

skills.grammar: finding your way: li rastê, li çepê, rasterast, li quncikê; transport words; bajar becomes bajêr after a preposition (li bajêr)
skills.grammarMd:
In the city you need the words for the way:

- **li rastê** on the right · **li çepê** on the left · **rasterast** straight on · **li quncikê** at the corner
- *Dikan li rastê ye.* The shop is on the right.
- *Rawestgeh li quncikê ye.* The stop is at the corner.

A few nouns change their vowel after a preposition: **bajar → bajêr**: *Ez li bajêr im.* I am in the city. · *Em ji bajêr tên.* We are coming from the city.

**bi** + vehicle is *by*: *bi otobûsê* by bus · *bi traktorê* by tractor · *bi minîbûsê* by minibus.

lessons.beat: Ferhad’s tractor rattles them to the main road, Bozo’s hat on Hevalo’s head; there a minibus driver squeezes everyone in and sells Hamo a ticket for the whole family.
In Amed every street looks like the last one. Hamo reads the signs aloud and turns left every time the sign says right.
The black walls of old Amed rise in front of them. Hamo stares at the traffic, Xezal is proud of her city, and Hevalo nearly disappears into a fruit stand.
Up four floors of stairs to Xezal’s flat; Hamo stops on every landing to “admire the view”. Gulîstan opens the door, and brother and sister look at each other: “Xezîne?” She smiles: “Li cem min e.”

skills.grammar: the imperative: bi- + present stem + -e (one person) / -in (more): bike, bixwe, bibêje; were, here, rûne, rabe; the negative with me-: meke, meçe
skills.grammarMd:
To tell someone to do something, use **bi-** + the present stem + **-e** (to one person) or **-in** (to more):

- *kirin → bike / bikin* do! · *xwarin → bixwe / bixwin* eat! · *gotin → bibêje* say! · *dan → bide* give!
- *nêrîn → binêre!* look! · *sekinîn → bisekine!* wait!

Some are short and irregular: **were** come! · **here** go! · **rûne** sit down! · **rabe** get up! · **vexwe** drink!

For *don’t*, put **me-** in place of bi-: *meke!* don’t! · *meçe!* don’t go! · *mexwe!* don’t eat! · *metirse!* don’t be afraid!

Polite: *Kerem bike, rûne.* Please, sit down. · *Werin, werin!* Come in, come in!

lessons.beat: Gulîstan’s welcome fills the stairwell: “Werin, werin! Rûnin!” Hamo is told to sit, get up, take off his shoes, sit again — by his little sister, exactly as when they were children.

new.en: to go out, to come out

lessons.beat: At Gulîstan’s table the orders never stop: “Bixwe! Vexwe! Bide min! Binêre!” Hamo eats everything he is given and is given everything again.
Hamo wants four sugars in his tea, a nap on the sofa and to phone the whole village on Gulîstan’s phone. Xezal: “Meke! Meke! Meke!” Gulîstan laughs until she cries.
Gulîstan brings out her own tin: the other half of the photo — and a note in their father’s hand. “Li Newrozê, li ser girê…” At Newroz, on the hill… The rest is smudged.

skills.grammar: divê and dikarim with the subjunctive: bi- + present stem + the personal ending (divê ez biçim, ez dikarim bêm, bila ew bixwe)
skills.grammarMd:
After **divê** (must), **dikarim** (I can) and **bila** (let), the next verb is in the **subjunctive**: **bi-** + present stem + ending.

- *Divê ez biçim.* I must go. · *Divê tu bixwî.* You must eat.
- *Ez dikarim alîkariya te bikim.* I can help you.
- *Bila ew rûne.* Let him sit down.

It looks like the imperative with person endings: *biçim, biçî, biçe, biçin*.

Some are irregular: *hatin → bêm, bêyî, bê, bên* · *vexwarin → vexwim* · *rûniştin → rûnim* · *rabûn → rabim* · *vegerîn → vegerim*.

Not: *Divê ez neçim.* I must not go. · *Ez nikarim bêm.* I can’t come.

lessons.beat: Hamo makes a list of everything he must do in Amed: see the walls, buy a book, eat the city’s bread — and find the hill in his father’s note.

new.en: let (bila ew bê: let him come)

lessons.beat: Gulîstan asks who can help her in the kitchen. Everybody can — except Hamo, who suddenly must rest. Xezal asks permission to take him to the bookshop instead.
Hamo wants a book of proverbs and asks the bookseller for one “his father would have liked”. He leaves with three books and a book of children’s stories for Hevalo, about apples.
Hamo goes out for bread and gets lost. Xezal guides him by phone, street by street: “Here rasterast… paşê li çepê…” He arrives an hour later — with the bread, and with new friends from the bakery.

skills.grammar: transport with bi (bi trênê, bi balafirê, bi peyatî) and polite requests in the city: ji kerema xwe, ez dixwazim …, dikarî …?
skills.grammarMd:
To say how you travel, use **bi** + the vehicle in the oblique:

- *Ez bi otobûsê diçim.* I go by bus. · *Em bi trênê tên.* We are coming by train.
- **bi peyatî** on foot: *Em bi peyatî diçin.* We are walking.

Asking politely:

- *Ji kerema xwe, otobûs li ku ye?* Where is the bus, please?
- *Tu dikarî alîkariya min bikî?* Can you help me?
- *Ez dixwazim bilêtekê bikirim.* I would like to buy a ticket.

**çiqas?** is *how much, how far*: *Çiqas dûr e?* How far is it?

lessons.beat: Baran wants to go home by train, Hêvî by plane, Hevalo on foot through the orchards. Hamo says they will go home the way they came: by minibus and tractor.
At the bus station Hamo queues for tickets and is very, very polite; the man behind the window is so charmed that he gives him the best seats.
Hamo asks a passer-by the way to the station — and the stranger turns out to be from the next village to Sêvan. They drink tea together and forget the time entirely.
The last evening in Amed. Gulîstan will come to the village for Newroz; Xezal packs; Hevalo has packed only apples. Then the news on the radio: snow is coming, and the mountain road may close.

units.story: They reach Sêvan just before the snow closes the pass, and the village waits out the last of the winter by the stove. Then the sun comes back, the snow melts, the streams roar and the whole family gets ready for Newroz: Nazê sews new clothes, Baran gathers firewood, Xezal plans the govend and Hamo practises a speech that nobody wants to hear. The future is on everyone’s lips — ez ê …, em ê … — and what everyone wants to do. On Newroz night, by the fire on their father’s hill, Hamo and Gulîstan lift a flat stone and find a shepherd’s flute and a note: keep the song going. The next morning Hamo cannot get out of bed.

skills.grammar: the weather: hewa sar e, baran dibare, berf dibare, roj derdikeve, ba tê; the seasons bihar, havîn, payîz, zivistan
skills.grammarMd:
Ask **Hewa çawa ye?** — What is the weather like?

- *Hewa sar e.* It is cold. · *Hewa germ e.* It is warm.
- *Baran dibare.* It is raining (the rain falls). · *Berf dibare.* It is snowing.
- *Roj derdikeve.* The sun is coming out. · *Ba tê.* The wind is blowing.
- *Hewa ewrî ye.* It is cloudy.

The seasons: *bihar* spring · *havîn* summer · *payîz* autumn · *zivistan* winter. “In winter” is **di zivistanê de** or simply **zivistanê**: *Zivistanê berf gelek e.* In winter there is a lot of snow.

lessons.beat: The minibus climbs the pass in the first snow. Hamo, who has seen sixty winters, describes the weather to the driver as if the driver had never seen any.
Snowed in at home, Hamo tells the children about the four seasons of Sêvan — mostly about what you eat in each of them.
The village is cut off by snow. Xezal and Hamo watch from the window: will it melt before Newroz? Outside, Hevalo builds a snow deer with a carrot for a nose, and eats the nose.
The sun returns, the snow melts and the stream by the walnut tree sings again. Hamo announces “Newroz tê!” — and Dapîr says that at Newroz she has something to tell them, about the photo.

skills.grammar: the future: ez ê, tu yê, ew ê, em ê, hûn ê + the subjunctive (ez ê biçim, em ê bibînin); also dê (ez dê bêm)
skills.grammarMd:
The future is the **subjunctive** with **ê** after the subject:

- *Ez ê biçim.* I will go. · *Em ê bibînin.* We will see.
- *Tu yê bêyî?* Will you come? (**yê** after a vowel)
- *Ew ê çay vexwe.* She will drink tea.

In writing you also see **dê**: *Ez dê sibe bêm.* I will come tomorrow.

Not: *Ez ê neçim.* I will not go. · *Ew ê nexwe.* He won’t eat.

Time words for the future: *sibe* tomorrow · *hefteya bê* next week · *sala bê* next year · *piştre* afterwards.

lessons.beat: Newroz is coming. Hamo hands out the jobs: Baran will collect firewood, Nazê will sew, Xezal will plan the govend, and he himself will… supervise.
Xezal makes plans for the future — Newroz, the summer, next year’s exams — and dreams aloud of teaching children one day. Hamo listens and says nothing, which is unusual.
Baran asks what Newroz really is. Hamo tells the old tale of Kawa the blacksmith, who lit fires on the hills to bring back the spring — a tale that grows longer every year he tells it.
Hamo practises his Newroz speech in front of the hens. The hens leave. Then his speech is gone too — and Hevalo is chewing something papery.

skills.grammar: dixwazim with the subjunctive (ez dixwazim govendê bigirim), dixwazim ku tu … (I want you to …), and hez dikim … bikim
skills.grammarMd:
**dixwazim** (I want) is followed by a verb in the subjunctive:

- *Ez dixwazim biçim.* I want to go.
- *Tu dixwazî govendê bigirî?* Do you want to dance the govend?

To want **someone else** to do it, add **ku** and their subject:

- *Ez dixwazim ku tu bêyî.* I want you to come.
- *Xezal dixwaze ku Hamo serçopî be.* Xezal wants Hamo to lead the dance. (**be**: the subjunctive of “is”)

The same works with *divê* and *dikarim*, which you know, and with *hez dikim*: *Ez hez dikim stranan bibêjim.* I like singing songs.

lessons.beat: Xezal teaches Baran and Hêvî the govend steps in the yard, with Hamo’s old radio for music; the hens dance too, in their way.
Nazê has sewn new clothes for everyone: a dress for Hêvî, a waistcoat for Baran, and for Hamo a new green pştên that he wears straight away, over his pyjamas.
Xezal wants Hamo to lead the govend at the front of the line. Hamo says his knees are too old. Xezal says his moustache is not. Hamo agrees to lead.

new.en: leader of the govend (at the head of the line)

lessons.beat: Everything is ready. The forecast says rain; Hamo says “Baran bereket e” — rain is a blessing. At midnight Hevalo sees a small light moving on the hill.

skills.grammar: wishes with be: Newroza we pîroz be!, Destê te sax be!; the future and the subjunctive in a celebration
skills.grammarMd:
Many Kurdish wishes end with **be**, the subjunctive of “is”: *may it be…*

- *Newroza we pîroz be!* Happy Newroz (to you all)! — answered with *Ya we jî pîroz be!*
- *Cejna te pîroz be!* Happy holiday!
- *Destê te sax be!* Bless your hands! (thanks for food or work)
- *Rojbûna te pîroz be!* Happy birthday!

On the day itself everyone speaks in the future: *Em ê agir vêxin. Ciwan ê di ser agir re baz bidin. Em ê govendê bigirin.* We will light the fire. The young will jump over it. We will dance.

lessons.beat: Newroz morning: rain, then sun. The whole village climbs to the hill for the seyran; at dusk Hamo lights the fire and the young people jump over it, one by one, in the smoke.

new.en: to light (a fire), to switch on

lessons.beat: Wishes everywhere: everyone wishes everyone a happy Newroz, health and success. Hamo thanks Nazê for the food with “Destê te sax be!” — and gives a speech after all, from memory.

new.en: Bless your hands! (thanks for food or work)

lessons.beat: By the dying fire Hamo, Gulîstan and Dapîr lift a flat stone where their father’s note said. Inside a tin: his shepherd’s flute, and a note — “Stranê bidomînin.” Keep the song going. Dapîr quietly wipes a tear.
Hamo tries the flute: a terrible squeak, and Hevalo’s ears go flat. Then Dapîr plays it perfectly, an old tune from the pastures. The next morning Hamo cannot get out of bed: his back!

units.story: After all that govend, Hamo’s back has given up, and Hamo turns out to be the most dramatic patient in the valley. Xezal nurses him, the family fusses, and the doctor who comes up from the town is Şîrîn, his old schoolmate, who beat him at every race when they were children and still teases him about it. Body words, aches and feelings, the doctor’s questions (“Ez te dibînim — where does it hurt?”) and a village moustache contest with comparisons and superlatives. Honey is forbidden; a jar goes missing; a moustache is sticky. Hamo gets better — but Baran comes home late one evening, muddy and silent, and will not say what happened.

skills.grammar: the body, and saying what hurts: … min diêşe (serê min diêşe), … min diêşin for more than one (lingên min diêşin)
skills.grammarMd:
To say something hurts, the body part is the subject of **êşîn** (to hurt):

- *Serê min diêşe.* My head hurts.
- *Pişta wî diêşe.* His back hurts.
- *Lingên min diêşin.* My legs hurt. (**diêşin** for more than one)
- *Çi diêşe?* What hurts? · *Li ku derê diêşe?* Where does it hurt?

The body part takes the ezafe and the owner: *destê min* my hand · *çavên te* your eyes · *guhê wê* her ear.

Other ways to feel unwell: *Ez nexweş im.* I’m ill. · *Taya min heye.* I have a fever. · *Ez ne baş im.* I’m not well.

lessons.beat: Hamo lies in bed and lists every part of himself that hurts, starting at his head and ending, after some time, at his toes.
Nazê asks him where exactly it hurts. Everywhere, says Hamo: his shoulders, his neck, his chest, even his little finger. Nazê raises one eyebrow — exactly the way Hamo does.
Xezal nurses her uncle: medicine, rest, no getting up. Hamo wants tea, honey and sympathy, in that order, and complains in a voice so weak that it can be heard in the next village.
Xezal phones the doctor in the town; Hamo hides the honey under his pillow. A knock: at the door stands Doctor Şîrîn — his old schoolmate, who beat him at every race when they were nine.

skills.grammar: pronoun objects in the present: the object pronoun comes before the verb (ez te dibînim, tu min dibînî, doktor wî kontrol dike); ji … hez kirin with a pronoun (ez ji te hez dikim); jê for ji wî / ji wê
skills.grammarMd:
In the present the object comes **before** the verb, and pronoun objects use the oblique forms you know: **min, te, wî, wê, me, we, wan**.

- *Ez te dibînim.* I see you.
- *Tu min nas dikî?* Do you know me?
- *Doktor wî kontrol dike.* The doctor examines him.
- *Em wan dibînin.* We see them.

With prepositions too: *ji min re* for me · *bi te re* with you · *Ez ji te hez dikim.* I love you.

**ji + wî / wê** is often shortened to **jê**: *Ez jê hez dikim.* I like him (her, it). · *Ez jê ditirsim.* I am afraid of it.

lessons.beat: Doctor Şîrîn examines Hamo: heart, breath, back. She listens, she presses, she frowns. Then she laughs: “Nexweşiya te ne ciddî ye — tu tenê pîr dibî!”

new.en: to beat (of the heart); to hit

lessons.beat: Xezal tells Hamo that everybody loves him — even when he is impossible. Hamo is touched, then annoyed at being touched, then touched again.

new.en: from him, from her, from it (ji + wî/wê)

lessons.beat: Şîrîn and Hamo remember their school days; she still teases him about the races. The prescription: rest, a walk every day, and no honey at night. Xezal writes it all down, delighted.
The villagers visit Hamo, each with a jar of honey; Xezal confiscates every jar and puts Hevalo on guard. In the morning one jar is empty — and Hamo’s moustache is suspiciously sticky.

skills.grammar: comparatives with -tir and ji (Baran ji Hêviyê mezintir e), the superlative with herî (çiyayê herî bilind, ya herî baş); çêtir as the comparative of baş
skills.grammarMd:
Add **-tir** to an adjective for *more …*, and use **ji** for *than*:

- *Baran ji Hêviyê mezintir e.* Baran is older than Hêvî.
- *Amed ji Sêvanê mezintir e.* Amed is bigger than Sêvan.
- *Simbêlê Hamo ji yê Ferhad dirêjtir e?* Is Hamo’s moustache longer than Ferhad’s?

**baş** has its own: **çêtir** better (also *baştir*).

For *the most …* put **herî** before the adjective, after the ezafe:

- *çiyayê herî bilind* the highest mountain
- *sêva herî şîrîn* the sweetest apple
- *Ev ya herî baş e.* This is the best one.

lessons.beat: Back on his feet, Hamo compares everyone in the family: who is taller, older, stronger, cleverer. He is, according to him, the best at everything except getting up.
Hamo asks everyone their favourite: the best season, the sweetest fruit, the most beautiful place. Hevalo’s answer to every question is the same.
The village moustache contest at the tea house, with Şîrîn as judge. Hamo is certain he will win. Ferhad’s is longer. Hamo’s, he announces, is “the most beautiful”, and the room agrees, laughing.
Hamo is better, and walks every day with Xezal and Hevalo. The best medicine of all, he says, is the air of the summer pastures. Then Baran comes home late, covered in mud, and will not say a word.

skills.grammar: feelings with the present and with pronoun objects: ez ditirsim, ez li te dinêrim, guhdariya min bike; xwe for the subject itself (ew bi xwe dikene)
skills.grammarMd:
Many feelings are said with an adjective and the copula, or with **bûn** (become) in the present:

- *Ez ditirsim.* I’m afraid. · *Ez ji gur ditirsim.* I’m afraid of the wolf.
- *Ez aciz dibim.* I’m getting bored. · *Ew dilxweş dibe.* She is cheering up.

Feelings towards someone use the pronoun objects and the prepositions:

- *Ez li te dinêrim.* I’m looking at you.
- *Guhdariya min bike!* Listen to me!
- *Ez te fêm dikim.* I understand you.

**xwe** is the subject’s own: *Ew bi xwe dikene.* He laughs at himself. · *Baran li xwe dinêre.* Baran looks at himself.

lessons.beat: Baran sits alone on the roof. Hamo climbs up, slowly, his back complaining at every step, and sits beside him without a word, the way his own father used to.
Hamo tells Baran that he does not have to talk — only listen. He talks about trust, and about how hard it was, at nine, to tell his own father the truth.

new.en: to listen (guhdariya … kirin: to listen to)

lessons.beat: Xezal gently asks Baran what is wrong. He only says “Sibe ez ê bibêjim.” Then Hevalo sits next to him and offers him his last apple — and that, everyone agrees, is a very big moment.
By the stove Hamo tells Xezal how, as a boy, he lost his father’s best ram on the pastures and hid for a whole day. Brave people, he says, are the ones who tell. In the morning Baran begins: “Duh…”

units.story: Baran finally tells what happened yesterday: he took Bozo to the river, Bozo saw a goat and ran off up the valley, Baran followed, got lost, sat down under a walnut tree and fell asleep — and came home in the dark by the stars, to find that Bozo had been home for hours, eating Dapîr’s mint. Then everyone tells their own yesterday, and Hamo tells the stories of long ago: the wolf he met at nine (it gets bigger every time; Dapîr says it was a dog), the old days at the pastures, Dapîr’s own youth. A message comes down from Bişar the shepherd: a strange visitor comes to his tent every night. Hamo decides: this summer, the whole family goes up to the zozan.

skills.grammar: the past of intransitive verbs: past stem + -im, -î, —, -in (ez çûm, tu hatî, ew rabû, em man); the negative with ne- (neçûm, nehat)
skills.grammarMd:
Verbs that take no object (go, come, sit, sleep…) make their past from the **past stem** with the personal endings:

| | çûn (go) | hatin (come) |
|---|---|---|
| ez | çûm | hatim |
| tu | çûyî | hatî |
| ew | çû | hat |
| em, hûn, ew | çûn | hatin |

The past stem is the dictionary form without **-n**: *çûn → çû*, *rabûn → rabû*, *ketin → ket*, *mayîn → ma*.

**Not** is **ne-** in front: *Ez neçûm.* I didn’t go. · *Ew nehat.* He didn’t come.

*Duh çi bû?* What happened yesterday? · *Ez duh çûm bazarê.* I went to the market yesterday.

lessons.beat: At breakfast Baran takes a deep breath: “Duh ez çûm çem…” The whole table goes quiet. Even the kettle seems to stop.
Baran goes on: Bozo saw a goat on the other side of the valley and ran. Baran ran after him, over the stones, along the cliffs, up and up the valley.
Xezal asks the questions everyone is afraid to ask. Baran admits it: he lost Bozo, then lost himself, sat down under a walnut tree to think — and fell asleep.

When Baran woke it was dark, so he followed the stars home, as Hamo once taught him. And Bozo? Bozo had come home alone, hours before, and eaten all of Dapîr’s mint. But Baran saw something in the valley: smoke from a tent where nobody lives.

new.en: went out, came out (past of derketin)

skills.grammar: time in the past: duh, pêr, par, berê, wê demê, hefteya borî, … berî niha (sê roj berî niha); dema ku … (when …)
skills.grammarMd:
Words that put a story in the past:

- *duh* yesterday · *pêr* the day before yesterday · *par* last year · *berê* before, in the old days
- *hefteya borî* last week · *sala borî* last year · *wê demê* at that time
- *sê roj berî niha* three days ago · *bîst sal berî niha* twenty years ago

**dema ku** (or just **dema**) joins two things that happened at the same time: *Dema ku ez zarok bûm, em li zozanan bûn.* When I was a child, we were on the summer pastures.

**hebû** is the past of *heye*: *Gurek hebû.* There was a wolf. · *Hespekî me hebû.* We had a horse.

lessons.beat: Hamo sits back, strokes his moustache and begins the old days: “Dema ku ez zarok bûm, em her havîn li zozanan bûn…” Nazê pours more tea; this will take a while.
Xezal tells about her first year in Amed: she arrived, was lost for a week, passed every exam — and on the first day she started classes in the wrong building.
Hamo’s favourite story: at nine, alone on the pastures, he met a wolf as big as a horse. It was a bear. It was a lion. Dapîr, quietly: it was the shepherd’s dog.
Bişar the shepherd sends a message down from the pastures with a boy on a mule: a wild creature comes to his tent every night, like a deer, but shy as a shadow. Hevalo’s ears shoot straight up.

skills.grammar: telling events in order: pêşî, paşê, piştre, piştî ku …, berî ku … (+ subjunctive), di dawiyê de; more intransitive pasts (geriya, meşiya, kenî, sekinî)
skills.grammarMd:
To tell what happened in order:

- **pêşî** first · **paşê / piştre** then, afterwards · **di dawiyê de** in the end
- **piştî ku** + past: *Piştî ku em gihîştin, me çay vexwar.* After we arrived, we drank tea.
- **berî ku** + subjunctive: *Berî ku ez razim, ez dixwînim.* Before I go to sleep, I read.

More pasts: *ez geriyam* I walked around · *ew meşiya* she walked · *em kenîn* we laughed · *ew sekinî* he stopped · *çivîk firiya* the bird flew.

A day in a few words: *Pêşî ez rabûm. Paşê ez çûm baxçe. Di dawiyê de ez vegeriyam malê.*

lessons.beat: Hamo teaches Baran how to tell a story properly — first, then, after that, in the end — using the most exciting day of his life: the day he bought Bozo.
Hamo retells Baran’s day in order, and it becomes a hero’s journey: Baran walked, wandered, stopped, laughed at his fear, and slept like a shepherd under the stars.

At dinner everyone tells their yesterday in order. Dapîr went to the neighbours and stayed till night; Hêvî’s cat had three kittens; Xezal’s bus was late. Hamo: “I sat. I drank tea. I slept.” Laughter all round.

new.en: to be born, to come about

lessons.beat: Hamo makes a decision: this summer the whole family will move up to the pastures to see Bişar and his mysterious visitor. The packing begins at once — and Bozo, hearing the word “zozan”, runs away again.

new.en: to move house, to migrate (with the flocks)

skills.grammar: a story in the past: hebû and tunebû (there was / was not), the negative past (neçû, nehat, nebû), and chains of intransitive pasts with û, paşê and dema ku
skills.grammarMd:
Every Kurdish tale starts in the past with **hebû** — *Hebû tunebû…* Once upon a time (there was, there wasn’t).

- *Kerekî me hebû.* We had a donkey.
- *Li gund dibistan tunebû.* There was no school in the village.

Chain the events with **û** and **paşê**: *Ez rabûm, derketim û ber bi çiyê ve meşiyam.* I got up, went out and walked towards the mountain.

The negative past puts **ne-** before the verb: *Bozo nehat.* Bozo didn’t come. · *Em neçûn.* We didn’t go. · *Ew dereng nema.* She didn’t stay late.

With a compound verb the ne- goes on the verb part: *Ez siwar nebûm.* I didn’t ride.

lessons.beat: Dapîr, packing her old saddlebags, tells what she did not do at Baran’s age: she did not go to school, she did not get off a horse all summer, and she never got lost.

new.en: to rise (of the sun, the moon)
to go down, to get off
there was; (someone) had (the past of heye)

lessons.beat: Hamo tries to show how organised the family will be, and tells how, the last time they moved to the pastures, he was late by one whole day — by mistake, of course, completely by mistake.
Xezal and Baran search for Bozo, calling his name up the valley; Hevalo follows his tracks. They find him at the spring with Ferhad’s donkey, very much in love.

The evening before they leave, Dapîr tells how, as a girl, she rode up to the pastures every summer with her mother, and how the young people danced at weddings there. At dawn the family sets off — and halfway up, a flock of sheep blocks the path, led by a shepherd who looks very familiar.

units.story: The familiar shepherd on the path is Bişar, and he leads the family up to the zozan, the high summer pastures, where his black tents stand by a cold spring. Life up there is milk and bread and work: milking at dawn, churning butter, baking bread on the saj, songs at night under more stars than Baran can count. The mysterious visitor is a wild doe, Zerê, who comes for salt — and for Hevalo, who gives her his apples. Following the two deer, the family finds a hidden lake and an old stone house: Dapîr’s summer home when she was a girl, where Hamo’s father once played his flute for her. The past now has objects — min nan xwar, te çi kir?, me ew dîtin — and memories run in the past continuous. On the way down, Xezal’s phone finds a signal and a job offer, far away.

skills.grammar: the past of transitive verbs is ergative: the doer takes the oblique (min, te, wî, wê, me, we, wan) and the verb uses the past stem (min nan xwar, te çi kir?, wê got)
skills.grammarMd:
With verbs that take an object (eat, see, say, do…) the past works differently. The **doer** is in the oblique — the same **min, te, wî, wê, me, we, wan** you know from *navê min* — and the verb is the **past stem**:

- *Min nan xwar.* I ate bread.
- *Te çi kir?* What did you do?
- *Wî çay vexwar.* He drank tea.
- *Me ew dît.* We saw him.

A noun doer is oblique too: a feminine one takes -ê (*Xezalê got …* Xezal said …), a plural -an (*zarokan got …* the children said …); masculine names usually stay as they are (*Hamo got …*).

The past stems: *xwar* (ate) · *vexwar* (drank) · *kir* (did) · *got* (said) · *dît* (saw) · *da* (gave) · *anî* (brought) · *bir* (took away) · *xwest* (wanted).

Not: *Min nexwar.* I didn’t eat. · *Wê negot.* She didn’t say.

lessons.beat: The shepherd on the path is Bişar, Hamo’s old friend. They drink tea on the rocks while the sheep go past, and Hamo tells him everything that happened on the way — twice.

new.en: to lift; to take away, to clear

lessons.beat: At the tents Bişar asks everyone what they saw on the climb. Baran saw an eagle; Hêvî saw a hundred flowers; Hamo saw nothing, because he was talking.
At dusk, Xezal and you spot two deer at the edge of the meadow. The doe stops and looks straight at Hevalo; Hevalo drops his apple. Xezal whispers: “Min dît! Te jî dît?”
By the fire Bişar tells how the doe comes every night for the salt he puts out; Hamo names her Zerê, “the golden one”. In the morning Hevalo is gone — and so is the sack of apples.

skills.grammar: ergative agreement: the past verb agrees with the object — min sêv xwar (one apple), min sêv xwarin (apples); wî ez dîtim, min tu dîtî, me hûn dîtin
skills.grammarMd:
In the transitive past the verb agrees with the **object**, not with the doer:

- *Min sêvek xwar.* I ate an apple. · *Min du sêv xwarin.* I ate two apples. (**-in** for a plural object)
- *Wî ez dîtim.* He saw me. (**-im**: the object is *ez*)
- *Min tu dîtî.* I saw you.
- *Me hûn dîtin.* We saw you (all).

So the object goes into the direct form (*ez, tu, ew, em, hûn*) and the doer into the oblique (*min, te, wî, wê, me, we, wan*) — the opposite of the present: *Ez te dibînim* / *Min tu dîtî*.

More past stems: *dot* (milked) · *çêkir* (made) · *pijand* (cooked) · *şûşt* (washed) · *xwend* (read) · *nivîsî* (wrote) · *kirî* (bought).

lessons.beat: Dawn on the zozan: Bişar teaches you to milk a ewe, and Dapîr shows Nazê how her mother churned butter in a goatskin. Hamo milks one ewe, proudly, and spills half of it.

new.en: milkmaid (the woman who milks the flock)

lessons.beat: Xezal catches Hevalo slipping away to the meadow with an apple in his mouth. “Min tu dîtî!” He pretends he did not see her see him.
Dapîr and Nazê bake bread on the saj over the fire. Hamo “helps” and burns one; Bişar teases him for an hour. Then Baran notices: the doe’s tracks lead away from the camp — and Hevalo’s go with them.

new.en: to take out, to bring out

lessons.beat: The whole camp searches. At last they find the two deer high above the tents, at a hidden lake, sharing apples. Bişar says nobody has seen this lake for fifty years — and there is an old stone house beside it.

skills.titleEn: I was eating, I was going
skills.grammar: the past continuous: di- + past stem, for what used to happen or was happening (min dixwar, ez diçûm, wan digot, me dilîst); dema ku … with the past continuous
skills.grammarMd:
For what **was happening** or **used to happen**, put **di-** before the past stem:

- *Ez diçûm.* I was going / I used to go.
- *Min nan dixwar.* I was eating bread.
- *Dapîr her havîn dihat vir.* Grandma used to come here every summer.
- *Wan stran digotin.* They were singing songs.

The agreement rules stay the same: intransitive with the subject, transitive with the object.

Two at once: *Dema ku me nan dixwar, Zerê hat.* While we were eating, Zerê came.

Negative: **ne-** before di-: *Min nedizanî.* I didn’t know. · *Em nediçûn wir.* We didn’t use to go there.

lessons.beat: Hamo tells you how it used to be: when he was little, the whole village came up here every summer, the women milked, the men made cheese, and the children played in the river all day.

new.en: was …-ing, used to (the past continuous: diçûm, min dixwar)
to raise, to keep (animals); to look after

lessons.beat: In the old stone house Dapîr stops at the door. This was her family’s summer home when she was a girl; she used to swim in the lake and dry curd on that very roof.
Dapîr tells: while the women were milking, the girls used to sing; one night a young shepherd played a flute by the lake — Hamo’s father. Hamo, for once in his life, has nothing to say.

new.en: asking for a girl’s hand (the betrothal visit)

lessons.beat: The last days on the zozan. Hevalo must say goodbye to Zerê; she nudges an apple back towards him, and then she is gone into the grass. On the way down Xezal’s phone finds a signal: dozens of messages, her exam results — and a job offer in Hewlêr.

skills.grammar: telling a whole day in the past, mixing the two kinds of verb (ez çûm û min … dît), questions in the past (te çi kir?, kê got?, çi qewimî?) and ji … re gotin (to tell someone)
skills.grammarMd:
A real story mixes the two pasts — check each verb:

- *Ez çûm mêrgê û min Zerê dît.* I went to the meadow and saw Zerê. (*çûn* intransitive → *ez*; *dîtin* transitive → *min*)
- *Em rûniştin û me nan xwar.* We sat down and ate bread.

Questions: *Te çi kir?* What did you do? · *Kê got?* Who said (it)? (**kê** is the oblique of *kî*) · *Çi qewimî?* What happened?

To tell **someone**, use **ji … re**: *Min ji te re got.* I told you. · *Xezalê ji diya xwe re got.* Xezal told her mother.

And to tell a whole tale, *vegotin*: *Hamo çîrokek vegot.* Hamo told a story.

lessons.beat: Back in Sêvan, everyone tells the summer at once. Who saw the lake first? Who burned the bread? Who said the doe was “just a goat”? Hamo says he does not remember saying that.
Xezal phones her mother and tells her the whole summer, the lake, the stone house, the flute. Gulîstan is silent for a long moment, and then asks to see every photo.
The family looks at the summer photos, one memory each: Hamo’s burned bread, Bozo’s third escape, Hevalo and Zerê at the lake. Hamo: “Me havîneke xweş derbas kir.”
Hamo writes the summer down in his old notebook, slowly, so nothing is lost. Baran asks what comes next. Xezal is quiet all evening, and then she says: “Xalo, divê ez tiştekî ji te re bibêjim.”

units.story: Xezal finally says it: a school in Hewlêr has offered her a post as a teacher, and she is afraid to leave — the village, her mother, her uncle. Hamo goes quiet, strokes his moustache, and then smiles, though his eyes are wet. Over the autumn the family talks about work (everyone in the village has a trade, and an opinion), about school (Baran has to give a talk about Sêvan in front of the whole school, and is terrified), and about plans and dreams. The present perfect says what has been done (min biryar daye) and the linking words say why (ji ber ku, loma, lê, dema ku). Xezal decides to go after the winter, and promises to come home for every Newroz. Hamo makes a plan of his own: every winter night, one of his father’s stories.

skills.grammar: jobs and the endings that make them: -kar / -ker (cotkar, karker), -van (rojnamevan), -dar (dikandar), -pêj (aşpêj); kar kirin, and bûn + a job (ez ê bibim mamoste)
skills.grammarMd:
Ask **Karê te çi ye?** What is your job? — *Ez mamoste me.* I am a teacher.

Many jobs are built from a word and an ending:

- **-kar / -ker**: *cot* plough → *cotkar* farmer · *kar* work → *karker* worker
- **-van**: *rojname* newspaper → *rojnamevan* journalist · *şivan* shepherd
- **-dar**: *dikan* shop → *dikandar* shopkeeper
- **-pêj**: *aşpêj* cook · *nanpêj* baker

To say what someone **becomes**, use *bûn*: *Ez dixwazim bibim mamoste.* I want to become a teacher. · *Ew bû endezyar.* She became an engineer.

Where: *Ew li nexweşxaneyê dixebite.* He works at the hospital.

lessons.beat: Hamo walks Baran through the village trades: Ferhad the farmer, the cook at the tea house, the builder who mended the mill — and Bişar, the best shepherd in the mountains.

lessons.titleEn: I want to become a teacher
lessons.beat: Xezal and Baran play “what will you be?”. Baran will be a pilot, a cook, a doctor and a shepherd. Xezal, quietly, says she has always wanted to be a teacher.
Xezal tells Hamo: a school in Hewlêr wants her as a teacher. Hamo is silent for a long time, strokes his moustache, and then smiles: “Ev nûçeyeke mezin e!” His eyes say something else.

The next day Hamo works in the orchard alone. Ferhad, Mîrza and Bişar stop by one after another, each telling him why his own work is the best in the world. Hamo listens — and calls a family council for that evening.

skills.grammar: the present perfect: past stem + -ime, -iyî, -iye, -ine after a consonant (ez hatime, ew hatiye), -me, -yî, -ye, -ne after a vowel (ez çûme, ew çûye); with transitive verbs min … kiriye, me … dîtiye
skills.grammarMd:
For what **has happened** (and still matters), add the copula-like endings to the past stem:

- after a consonant: *ez hatime, tu hatiyî, ew hatiye, em hatine* (I have come …)
- after a vowel: *ez çûme, tu çûyî, ew çûye, em çûne* (I have gone …)

Transitive verbs keep the ergative: *Min biryar daye.* I have decided. · *Te qet Hewlêr dîtiye?* Have you ever seen Hewlêr? · *Me sêv xwarine.* We have eaten (the) apples.

Useful with it: **tu car** never · **qet** ever / never · **heta niha** until now · **hê** / **hîn** still, yet: *Ez hê neçûme.* I have not gone yet.

Not: *ne-* before the stem: *Min nedîtiye.* I haven’t seen it.

lessons.beat: At the family council Hamo speaks first: he has thought, he has slept on it (twice), and he has decided — Xezal must take the job. Then he asks everyone else what they have decided.

new.en: has …ed (the present perfect: hatiye, min kiriye)

lessons.beat: Xezal asks Hamo if he has ever been to Hewlêr. Once, he says, thirty years ago: he has seen the citadel, the old bazaar and the main square — and has told the story at every wedding since.

Around the stove: Nazê, Dapîr, Baran, Hêvî, and Gulîstan on the phone. Each says what they have thought; Dapîr says she has seen eighty years and has never regretted a brave decision. It is agreed: Xezal will go.

lessons.titleKu: Ez ê biçim, lê ez ê vegerim
lessons.titleEn: I’ll go, but I’ll come back
lessons.beat: Xezal writes the school a letter: yes. Then Baran comes to her with a problem of his own: his teacher wants him to give a talk about the village in front of the whole school, and he is terrified.

skills.grammar: linking ideas: ji ber ku and çimkî (because), loma and ji ber vê yekê (so), lê and lêbelê (but), hem … hem (both … and), bêyî ku (without), her çend (although)
skills.grammarMd:
Join two thoughts with these:

- **ji ber ku / çimkî** because: *Ez diçim, ji ber ku ev derfeteke mezin e.* I am going because this is a big chance.
- **loma / ji ber vê yekê** so, that is why: *Baran ditirse, loma Hamo alîkariya wî dike.* Baran is afraid, so Hamo helps him.
- **lê / lêbelê** but, however: *Hewlêr dûr e, lê ez ê her Newrozê bêm.* Hewlêr is far, but I will come every Newroz.
- **hem … hem** both … and: *Ew hem mamoste ye hem jî nivîskar.* She is both a teacher and a writer.
- **bêyî ku** + subjunctive, without: *bêyî ku bifikire* without thinking
- **her çend** although: *Her çend ez ditirsim jî, ez ê biçim.* Although I am afraid, I will go.

lessons.beat: Hamo explains why he said yes, because by because: because Xezal is ready, because the children of Hewlêr need her, because his own father once let him go.
Baran lists the reasons he cannot give the talk: the hall is big, the children will laugh, his voice will shake. Hamo answers every “but” with a “however”.

Hamo helps Baran write his talk about Sêvan, full of becauses and so’s. Baran practises in front of the hens, as Hamo once did — and Hevalo, the most patient audience in the world, applauds with his hooves.
Baran gives his talk, and the whole school claps. His teacher, Hêlîn, praises him — and then turns to Xezal: they studied together in Amed, and she has news about the school in Hewlêr.

skills.grammar: talking about plans and hopes: hêvî dikim ku …, armanca min ev e ku …, dema ku + subjunctive for the future (dema ku ez biçim Hewlêrê, …)
skills.grammarMd:
For plans and hopes the subjunctive comes back after **ku**:

- *Hêvî dikim ku tu serkeftî bî.* I hope that you will be successful.
- *Armanca min ev e ku ez zimanê dayikê hînî zarokan bikim.* My goal is to teach children their mother tongue.

**dema ku** + subjunctive talks about the future: *Dema ku ez biçim Hewlêrê, ez ê her roj telefonî we bikim.* When I go to Hewlêr, I will phone you every day.

And the plain future for what is decided: *Em ê bên serdana te.* We will come to visit you.

Wishes for the road: *Bi xêr biçî!* Go well! · *Serkeftin!* Good luck!

lessons.beat: Hamo asks everyone about their goals. Baran wants to give another talk (!). Hêvî wants a cat. Nazê wants Hamo to be on time, once. Hamo hopes for a good harvest — and that Xezal will be happy.
Xezal plans her new life: a small rented room near the school, a new neighbourhood, new friends, a phone call home every Friday — and her mother tongue, taught to children every day.

new.en: a stranger; far from home, homesick

lessons.beat: By the orchard wall Hamo gives Xezal the words his father gave him when he left for the city as a young man: “Here, lê rehên xwe ji bîr meke.” Go, but don’t forget your roots.
The last winter before Xezal leaves. Hamo has a plan: every night by the stove, one of the tales his father told him, so she can carry them with her. The first night he begins: “Hebû tunebû…”

new.en: once upon a time (there was, there wasn’t)
a winter evening of stories and visits
dengbêj, the traditional singer of tales

units.story: The last winter by the stove. Each night Hamo tells one of his father’s tales — Şengê and Pengê and the wolf at the door, the fox who shared a field with the bear — while Dapîr answers every tale with a proverb and the children act them out (Hevalo makes a terrible wolf: too friendly). One snowy night travellers knock: a dengbêj and his daughter, who sing for their supper and turn out to have known Hamo’s father; their song about his flute is missing its last verse, until it is found on the back of an old note. Conditions (heke tu derî vekî …) and reported speech (wî got ku …) join everything the road has taught. Spring comes, and with it the farewell govend; at the blue gate where the road began, Hamo, Hevalo and you send Xezal off to Hewlêr: “Rêya te vekirî be!” And under the apple tree, a new sapling she planted for Hevalo.

skills.grammar: conditions with heke / eger + the subjunctive (heke tu derî vekî, gur tê hundir), and the subjunctive of “to be”: bim, bî, be, bin (heke tu birçî bî)
skills.grammarMd:
To say **if**, use **heke** (or **eger**) with the subjunctive:

- *Heke tu derî vekî, gur tê hundir.* If you open the door, the wolf comes in.
- *Heke baran bibare, em ê li malê bimînin.* If it rains, we will stay at home.
- *Eger tu bixwazî, ez ê alîkariya te bikim.* If you want, I will help you.

With “to be” the subjunctive is **bim, bî, be, bin**:

- *Heke tu birçî bî, were bixwe.* If you are hungry, come and eat.
- *Heke ew ne dayika me be, em derî venakin.* If she is not our mother, we won’t open the door.

The second half is often the present or the future: *… em naçin* / *… em ê neçin*.

lessons.beat: Hamo begins the first tale: a mother goat goes up to the pastures each morning and tells her two kids, Şengê and Pengê, never to open the door to anyone.
The wolf comes and sings in a soft voice, and Hamo stops to ask the children: what will happen if they open the door? Hêvî knows: “Heke ew ne dayika wan be…”

new.en: (that I) be; (if) I am (the subjunctive of “to be”)

lessons.beat: Xezal and Hêvî act the tale out for the family. Hevalo plays the wolf — badly: he is far too friendly and keeps offering apples through the door. Hêvî shouts “Tu ne dayika me yî!” and everyone claps.
Dapîr says every tale has a lesson, and gives a proverb for this one. Baran asks for another story. Then a loud knock at the door, in the middle of a snowy night.

skills.grammar: hospitality, and reported speech: got ku … (he said that …), pirsî ka … (she asked whether …), dibêjin ku … (they say that …)
skills.grammarMd:
To report what someone said, use **got ku** + the words, with the persons changed:

- Hamo: “Ez ê sibe bêm.” → *Hamo got ku ew ê sibe bê.* Hamo said that he would come tomorrow.
- Xezal: “Ez westiyayî me.” → *Xezalê got ku ew westiyayî ye.* Xezal said she was tired.

For a question, **pirsî ka** (asked whether): *Dapîrê pirsî ka mêvan birçî ne.* Grandma asked whether the guests were hungry.

**Dibêjin ku …** they say that …: *Dibêjin ku dengbêj bavê Hamo nas dikir.* They say the dengbêj knew Hamo’s father.

And at the door: *Bi xêr hatin!* Welcome (to you all)! · *Ser çavan!* With pleasure! · *Mala te ava!* Thank you (may your house prosper)!

lessons.beat: At the door stand two travellers caught by the snow: an old man with a long-necked tembûr and his daughter. Hamo does not even ask who they are: “Bi xêr hatin! Werin hundir!”

new.en: Is everything all right? What brings you?
the cloth a meal is laid on; a meal spread

lessons.beat: Over dinner Xezal translates between everyone who is talking at once: the old man said that…, Dapîr asked whether…, Hamo claims that… — until she gives up and laughs.
The old man is a dengbêj; he sings kilams of the old days in a voice that fills the house. Then he puts down his tembûr: he knew Hamo’s father, and used to sing with his flute.
Next morning the guests are gone, leaving a song about Hamo’s father’s flute. Xezal retells it all to Dapîr — who says the song is missing its last verse, and only one person ever knew it.

new.en: to remember, to call to mind

skills.grammar: proverbs and how they are built (… çiqas … be jî, …; the general present: … dibe, … derdixe), and a retold tale in the past with dialogue
skills.grammarMd:
Proverbs — **gotinên pêşiyan**, “the sayings of those before” — are short and often use the general present:

- *Mêvan mêvanê Xwedê ye.* The guest is God’s guest.
- *Zimanê şîrîn mar ji qulê derdixe.* A sweet tongue brings the snake out of its hole.
- *Dilop bi dilop gol çêdibe.* Drop by drop a lake is made.

**çiqas … be jî** means *however … it is*: *Çiya çiqas bilind be jî, rê di ser re heye.* However high the mountain, there is a way over it.

In a tale, the past and the dialogue come together: *Rovî got: “Tu kîjan dixwazî?” Hirçê got: “Yên li ser erdê!”* The fox said: “Which do you want?” The bear said: “The ones above the ground!”

lessons.beat: The second night: the fox and the bear share a field. Each year the bear chooses what is above the ground or below it, and each year the clever fox has planted the crop that leaves her the leaves, the roots or the stalks. Hamo does the bear’s voice.
Dapîr answers each tale with a proverb, and Hamo explains each proverb with another tale, which Dapîr answers with another proverb. Nobody goes to bed.

new.en: A sweet tongue brings the snake out of its hole.
Drop by drop a lake is made.

new.ku: Çiya çiqas bilind be jî, rê di ser re heye.
new.en: However high the mountain, there is a way over it.

lessons.beat: A proverb duel: Xezal against Dapîr, with Hamo as judge. Dapîr always has the last word. Then Hevalo invents one of his own: “Sêvek her roj, doktor ji derî dûr!” Nobody can say it isn’t true.

Dapîr remembers where the last verse is: on the back of their father’s Newroz note. They turn it over — there it is, in his hand, written for the grandchildren he never met. Hamo reads it aloud, and his voice shakes.

skills.grammar: everything together: present, past, future and wishes in one farewell (… pîroz be, … vekirî be, … sax be)
skills.grammarMd:
A farewell uses every tense you know:

- the past: *Tu salekê li vir mayî û tu bûyî endamê malbatê.* You stayed here a year and became one of the family.
- the present perfect: *Tu gelek tiştan fêr bûyî.* You have learned a lot.
- the future: *Em ê bêriya te bikin.* We will miss you.
- the subjunctive and wishes: *Rêya te vekirî be!* May your road be open! · *Xwedê ji te razî be!* God be pleased with you (thank you)! · *Bi silametî biçî û werî!* Go and come back safely!

And the answer to a goodbye: *Bi xatirê we!* — *Oxir be!* Good luck!

Heta dîtinê — until we meet again.

lessons.beat: Spring again, and the farewell party fills the square. Drums, zurnas and ululating; the govend winds round the square, Hamo at its head with his father’s handkerchief — and even Bozo, it is said, dances.
Xezal’s goodbye speech to the family: thank you for everything, for every tale, for every glass of tea. Then she turns to her uncle and cannot finish.
Dawn at the blue gate, where your road began. Hamo, Hevalo and you say goodbye to Xezal. “Rêya te vekirî be,” says Hamo. “Xalo, simbêlê xwe biparêze!” says Xezal. Hevalo gets the last apple.

new.en: Safe journey! (may your road be open)
Thank you! (may God be pleased with you)

lessons.beat: A card arrives from Hewlêr, all in Kurmancî, and Hamo reads it aloud — and you understand every word. Under the old apple tree a sapling has appeared: Xezal planted it for Hevalo before she left. The end of the road — and the beginning of yours.

new.en: to get used to; to learn
